To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the chemical shift of a phosphate‐coupled residue can be used as a spectroscopic probe for folding and binding in intrinsically disorderd proteins.

the 31 phosphorous (31P) chemical shift can be used to probe the folding of the SLRP–RNA complex and the phosphorylation of a single threonine in SLBP promotes the folding and assembly of the SLRP complex.

31P Nmr can be used to probe the chemical nature of phosphothreonine in the RNA binding protein, SLBP, and the chemical shift of the phosphate is a good spectroscopic indicator of phosphate‐coupled binding and folding processes in intrinsinsically disordered phosphoproteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of NMR spectroscopy to investigate the structural and dynamic properties of proteins and protein complexes.
the structural basis of protein phosphorylation and the role of protein phosphorylation in RNA‐binding processes.
the structure and dynamics, at the atomic level, of proteins and nucleic acids, and the interaction between the two.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phosphorylation of the threonine residue is not a prerequisite for RNA binding, but it may contribute to the folding of the SLIP‐1 RNA binding domain of human SLBP.
31P Nmr is not a suitable tool to probe protein phosphorylation.
the 31 P‐NMR chemical shift is a very good spectroscopic probe to characterize phosphate‐coupled binding processes in intriniscally disordered proteins.

the 31p chemical shift is an excellent probe for phosphate‐mediated folding and binding processes.
31P Nmr spectroscopy is an effective tool for characterizing the structure and dynamics for phosphorylated intrinsically disorded proteins.
